passages.t: A new governor, and an old plot
passages.happening:
Three days after arriving in his province, Festus goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem (verse 1). There the chief priests and the Jewish leaders bring their case against Paul (verse 2). They ask Festus, as a favour, to have Paul brought to Jerusalem, because they are planning to ambush and kill him on the way (verse 3).

Festus refuses. Paul is being held in Caesarea, and he himself is going back there soon (verse 4). “So if this man has done anything wrong, let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Porcius Festus is the new Roman governor of Judea. When he arrived is debated: most scholars place it between about AD 58 and 60, and some argue for a few years earlier. He governed only a short time. The Jewish historian Josephus reports that he died in office, and that in the gap before the next governor arrived, the high priest had James, the brother of Jesus, put to death, about AD 62. Acts does not tell that story.

A new governor's first visit to Jerusalem mattered. He needed the goodwill of the city's leaders to keep the peace. So it is telling that, two years after Paul's arrest, the first thing they ask for is Paul. Two years have passed, and the plan is the same as before: an ambush on the road (23:12-15).

The ‘chief priests and Jewish leaders’ here are the high-priestly families and the council's leading men, the same circle that had brought the charges before Felix. Luke means these leaders, not the Jewish people; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

Festus says no, perhaps simply because he will not be told what to do in his first week. But his refusal saves Paul's life.
passages.ot: The Psalms know the long memory of those who plot against the innocent: “They conspire, they lurk, they watch my steps while they wait to take my life” (Psalm 56:6). And they know where safety finally lies: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes” (Psalm 118:9). God used a Roman governor to protect Paul, as Proverbs says: “The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases” (Proverbs 21:1).
passages.asks: Two years had not cooled the plotters' hatred. Ask whether there is a grudge you have kept alive for a long time, and what it is costing you. And notice that a stranger's simple refusal saved Paul's life. Ask whether a small ‘no’ from you could protect someone.

passages.happening:
After eight or ten days in Jerusalem, Festus goes down to Caesarea. The next day he takes his seat on the judgment seat and has Paul brought in (verse 6). The Jews who have come down from Jerusalem stand around him, bringing “many serious charges that they could not prove” (verse 7).

Paul's defence is short: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Festus acts quickly. Felix had let the case sit for two years. Festus hears it the day after he gets back.

The accusers ‘who had come down from Jerusalem’ are the leaders and their party, the same men who had asked for Paul to be ambushed. Their charges are serious, but Luke says plainly that they could not prove them.

Paul's answer covers the three kinds of charge: the law of the Jews, the temple, and Caesar. On the first two, he has kept the law and honoured the temple. The third is new and dangerous. Tertullus had painted Paul as a troublemaker ‘all over the world’ (24:5), and to Roman ears that could sound like a crime against the emperor's peace. Paul says he has done nothing against Caesar either. He is not a rebel. That matters for the whole of Acts, which shows again and again that the followers of Jesus were not enemies of public order.
passages.ot: The Law required that a charge be proved: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). The Proverbs add a warning that fits every courtroom: “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17).
passages.asks: Paul answered many charges with one plain sentence. Ask whether, when you are accused, you can say simply what is true without piling up words. And ask whether you ever repeat charges against someone that no one has proved.

passages.happening:
But Festus, “wishing to do the Jews a favor”, asks Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?” (verse 9).

Paul answers, “I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well” (verse 10). If he has done anything deserving death, he does not refuse to die. But if the charges are false, no one has the right to hand him over to them. “I appeal to Caesar!” (verse 11).

Festus confers with his council and replies, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Festus needs the leaders' goodwill, so he offers them something: a trial in Jerusalem, with himself as judge. But Paul knows what Jerusalem means. Twice now men have planned to kill him on that road. And a governor who wants to please his accusers is not a safe judge. ‘The Jews’ in verse 9 and verse 10 are the leaders who brought the case, as in verse 2.

So Paul uses the last protection a Roman citizen had: the appeal to Caesar. ‘I appeal to Caesar’ is a legal formula, and it moved his case out of a provincial court to the emperor's. About sixty years later the same practice appears in a governor's letter: Pliny the Younger, governing Bithynia around AD 112, wrote to the emperor Trajan that some accused Christians were Roman citizens, and that he had marked them to be sent to Rome. Scholars still debate the exact legal steps in Paul's day, but Acts makes the main point clear. Once Paul appealed, and Festus had consulted his advisers, the governor could no longer hand him over to Jerusalem.

Caesar here is the emperor Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68. Today his name is linked with the killing of Christians, and rightly: after the great fire of Rome in July 64, he blamed the Christians, and many were put to death. But that was still years away. The early years of Nero's rule, when he was guided by advisers such as the philosopher Seneca, were remembered by Roman writers as a time of good government. When Paul appealed, Rome looked like a safer court than Jerusalem.

The appeal was still a risk. It meant a long voyage, a long wait, and a judgment that could not be undone. But Paul had been promised he would testify in Rome (23:11). The empire's own law became the road that carried him there.
passages.ot:
Paul's words, ‘I do not refuse to die’, echo the courage of Esther, who went to the king against the law and said, “And if I perish, I perish!” (Esther 4:16). He does not seek death, but he will not buy his life with a lie.

And the way a foreign ruler's law carries God's servant where God means him to go recalls Joseph's words to his brothers: “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20).
passages.hard:
Should a Christian use the law to protect himself, as Paul did? Paul could have gone quietly to Jerusalem and trusted God. Instead he used his legal rights.

Most readers see no conflict between faith and using the law wisely. Paul was not trying to escape justice: he said that if he deserved death he would not refuse it. He was refusing to be handed over to men who meant to murder him. Using a fair law to avoid an unfair death is not a lack of trust in God. And Luke tells it as the way God's promise of 23:11 was kept. Paul's letters also show him willing to give up his rights when they stood in the way of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). The text does not make a rule for every case, but it shows that the law can be a gift God uses.
passages.asks: Paul said that if he deserved death he would not refuse to die, and if he did not, no one had the right to hand him over. Ask whether you can be that clear about the difference between suffering for doing right and letting yourself be wronged for no reason. And ask how you might use whatever protections you have, not only for yourself, but for others who have none.

passages.t: Festus explains the case to King Agrippa
passages.happening:
Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice come to Caesarea to pay their respects to the new governor (verse 13). Festus lays out Paul's case before the king (verse 14). The chief priests and elders asked him to condemn the man (verse 15). He told them that “it is not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers and defend himself against their charges” (verse 16).

So he heard the case without delay (verse 17). But the accusers brought none of the crimes he expected (verse 18). “They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive” (verse 19). Not knowing how to judge such things, Festus offered a trial in Jerusalem (verse 20), but Paul appealed to the Emperor, so Festus is holding him until he can send him to Caesar (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
King Agrippa is Herod Agrippa II, the son of the Herod who killed James and died suddenly in Acts 12. Rome gave him lands to the north and east of Galilee, and also the right to oversee the temple in Jerusalem and to appoint the high priest. That made him the obvious man for a new Roman governor to ask about a Jewish religious case.

Bernice was his sister. She had been widowed, and she lived at her brother's court for long periods. Some ancient writers, among them Josephus and the Roman poet Juvenal, repeated rumours about the two of them. These were rumours, reported as gossip, and nothing in Acts suggests them. Later she became the companion of Titus, the Roman general who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 and later became emperor. Luke says none of this. He shows only a king and his sister coming in state to welcome a new governor.

Festus's account to Agrippa is mostly fair, and it shows how the case looked to a Roman. He had expected a real crime, a robbery or a rebellion. Instead he found an argument ‘regarding their own religion’. The Greek word can mean religion or superstition; in front of a Jewish king, Festus probably means it politely. And at the centre of the argument he found ‘a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive’. A Roman governor sums up the gospel in one line without knowing it. The whole case, from beginning to end, turns on the resurrection.

Festus does leave out one thing. He offered Paul a trial in Jerusalem, Luke told us, ‘wishing to do the Jews a favor’ (verse 9). To Agrippa he says he offered it because he was ‘at a loss’. It is a small polishing of his own part, as Lysias's letter was (23:26-30).
passages.ot:
Festus says it was ‘not the Roman custom’ to condemn a man unheard. Israel's law had said the same long before: “both parties to the dispute must stand in the presence of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 19:17), and judges were to “judge your neighbor fairly” (Leviticus 19:15).

A ruler who did not know how to judge recalls Solomon's prayer for wisdom: “give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9).
passages.asks: Festus summed up the case as a quarrel about ‘a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive’. Ask whether that is still the centre of the faith as you hold it. And ask whether you have ever let someone's past, or rumours about them, decide what you think of them before you knew them.

passages.t: Paul brought before Agrippa and Bernice
passages.happening:
Agrippa says, “I would like to hear this man myself,” and Festus answers that he will hear him tomorrow (verse 22). The next day Agrippa and Bernice come “with great pomp” into the hall, with the commanders and the leading men of the city, and Paul is brought in (verse 23).

Festus introduces him. The whole Jewish community, he says, has petitioned him about this man, in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer (verse 24). But he has found that Paul has done nothing deserving death, and since Paul has appealed to the Emperor, he has decided to send him (verse 25). The trouble is, he has nothing definite to write to “our sovereign one” about him (verse 26). “For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Picture the scene. The king and his sister in their royal robes. The commanders of the troops stationed at Caesarea. The leading men of the city. And in the middle, a prisoner in chains.

Festus has a practical problem. A governor who sent a prisoner to the emperor had to send a written report of the charges with him, and Festus has nothing he can write. He has found no crime. So the grand hearing is partly a way to get the help of an expert, King Agrippa, in writing his letter.

‘The whole Jewish community’ is Festus's way of speaking, and it is a governor's exaggeration. He means the leaders who petitioned him and the crowds they could gather. Many Jews had believed in Jesus, and others in the council had found nothing wrong with Paul (23:9). The note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

Festus calls the emperor ‘our sovereign one’. In Greek it is simply ‘the lord’, the normal way to refer to the emperor by Nero's day. Luke records it in the same book that calls Jesus Lord from beginning to end. Neither Festus nor Luke comments on the clash. The reader is left to notice it.

And notice the verdict again. Festus, like Lysias before him, says Paul has ‘done nothing worthy of death’. Luke is building a record. Every Roman official who examines Paul finds him innocent.
passages.ot: The pomp of the powerful and the prisoner before them recall the Servant in Isaiah, before whom “Kings will shut their mouths because of Him” (Isaiah 52:15). And the Psalms remind rulers of their limits: “Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save” (Psalm 146:3).
passages.asks: A room full of power and fine clothes gathered to look at a man in chains. Ask which of them was really free. And ask whether you are more impressed by pomp than you should be, and slower than you should be to honour faithfulness in plain clothes.
